text: How does a treadmill know how fast you're running? It counts. Let's take one apart.
Up front, a motor and its controller. A short drive belt and a heavy flywheel turn the front roller.
The running belt loops around two rollers and slides over a lubricated deck, sitting on rubber cushions that soften every landing.
Now the clever part. A small magnet on the roller sweeps past a sensor once per turn. Each pulse means one roller's circumference of belt.
So, speed equals roller r p m times circumference. A two and a half inch roller at seven hundred r p m: about five miles an hour.
Each foot strike brakes the belt. The controller sees the pulses slow down and pushes more current until the speed recovers. Belts still dip four to nine percent.
An incline motor turns a lead screw to tilt the deck. Pull the safety key, and the motor stops.
Why does it feel easier? There's no air to push through, and the belt pulls your feet back for you. A 1996 study found a one percent incline matches running outside.
What should we take apart next?
